correctness.rationale: The proof reduces every three-party zero-sum discrepancy vector to a two-parameter normal form, derives the exact norm identity, and exhaustively enumerates every positive common-denominator realization through the first reversing layer with exact arithmetic.

evidence: Gallagher defines the least-squares index, reviews Loosemore-Hanby, and explicitly states equality for two parties.
Gallagher motivates least squares by registering a few large discrepancies more strongly than many small ones and reports that different measures can alter election orderings.
Later comparison literature proves the pointwise inequality G<=L and characterizes equality by exactly one overrepresented and one underrepresented party.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These are the strongest adjacent results. Pointwise domination and two-party equality do not determine the first dimension where two elections can be oppositely ranked or the exact three-party feasible band.

originality.rationale: Prior work covers the definitions, two-party equality, general pointwise comparison, and empirical ranking differences. The inspected sources and targeted searches did not state the sharp three-party reversal geometry or denominator-11 first layer.
residual_risks: The full 1971 Loosemore-Hanby article was not available through the checked open route; only its abstract and metadata were inspected directly.
The elementary norm geometry may appear in an unindexed exercise, software test, or specialist note.
The denominator-11 result is tied to a common positive grid and does not cover unequal vote and seat denominators.

source_inspections.assessment: Strong adjacent prior art. It explicitly owns two-party equality and qualitative ranking sensitivity, but does not state the three-party exact band, reversal criterion, or denominator-11 boundary.
source_inspections.evidence: The paper defines the least-squares index as the square root of half the sum of squared vote-seat differences, states that with two parties it equals Loosemore-Hanby, and explains that otherwise it reacts more strongly to concentrated discrepancies.
source_inspections.material_read: Full-text pages 1-12, with particular attention to the Measures of Disproportionality section, Loosemore-Hanby discussion, Rae and Least Squares section, the two-party equality statement, and the motivation that least squares weights a few large discrepancies more strongly.
source_inspections.method: Institutional PDF text extraction after open-access retrieval attempts failed; a separate rendered PDF page from later electoral literature was inspected to verify the displayed Gallagher formula visually.

value.rationale: The indices are standard measures of electoral disproportionality and intentionally respond differently to dispersed versus concentrated representation errors. The theorem identifies the smallest party system where that design choice can change a strict election ranking, gives a complete three-party formula, and provides a finite exact benchmark for positive rational shares.
